title: Checkpoint: A New Republic
objective: After this level you can explain how Americans wrote a constitution, argued over it, and made it work in the republic's first decades.
summary: From the weak Articles to a country twice its size: a timeline from 1781 to 1813 ties the chapter together, and a closer look shows who the new republic worked for.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: from a Congress that could only ask to a doubled country.
cards.body: Americans rebuilt their government, learned to hand over power, and pushed west. Let’s line it up.

events.label: The Articles of Confederation take effect
The Great Compromise passes by one vote
The states ratify the Bill of Rights
The House elects Jefferson after a tie
The Louisiana Purchase doubles the country
Tecumseh is killed at the Thames

cards.headline: A republic that worked, for some
cards.body: Of the 55 delegates who took part in the convention, 39 signed a Constitution that balanced big and small states in two houses. It protected slavery without ever naming it, and Ona Judge had to flee the president’s own house to be free. Power passed peacefully between parties after 1800. The country doubled in 1803, on land still largely occupied by Native peoples. The new republic worked, but not for everyone.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How the weak Articles and Shays’ Rebellion led Americans to write a new Constitution in 1787.
How the Great Compromise and three slavery clauses shaped Congress and the Constitution.
Why the ratification fight produced the Bill of Rights, and why 1800’s handover mattered.
What the Louisiana Purchase and the War of 1812 meant for Native nations.

questions.prompt: A New Republic: which order of events is right?

options.label: The Louisiana Purchase, the Articles take effect, the Great Compromise
The Articles take effect, the Great Compromise, the Louisiana Purchase
The Great Compromise, the Articles take effect, the Louisiana Purchase
options.rationale: The Articles took effect first, in 1781.

options.label: The Articles take effect, the Louisiana Purchase, the Great Compromise

questions.explanation: The Articles took effect in 1781, the Great Compromise passed in 1787, and the Louisiana Purchase came in 1803.

options.label: Electors didn’t mark which vote was for president
Half the states refused to send their electors
options.rationale: The tie came from how electors voted.

options.label: The Senate split its vote evenly on the winner
options.rationale: The tie was in the electoral votes.

questions.explanation: Electors cast two votes without marking one for president, so the running mates tied at 73.

questions.prompt: How did the Constitution of 1787 handle slavery?

options.label: It abolished slavery everywhere
options.rationale: It protected slavery in several clauses.

options.label: It named slavery openly and banned it in the North
options.rationale: It never uses the word slavery.

options.label: It left slavery entirely out of its clauses
options.rationale: Several clauses dealt with it, without naming it.

options.label: It protected slavery without ever naming it

questions.explanation: Clauses on House seats, the slave trade and escapees protected slavery, but the words slave and slavery never appear.

questions.prompt: Who led the Shoshone band that helped the Corps of Discovery get horses?

options.label: Toussaint Charbonneau
options.rationale: He was Sacagawea’s husband, traveling with the Corps.

Tenskwatawa, the Prophet

questions.explanation: Sacagawea’s brother Cameahwait led the Shoshone band the Corps met in August 1805.

questions.prompt: Level 6’s Haudenosaunee council gave each nation one vote. Which part of the new US Congress gives each state an equal voice?

options.label: The House of Representatives
The Senate
The cabinet
options.rationale: The cabinet advises the president; it isn’t part of Congress.

options.label: Neither house
options.rationale: The Senate gives every state equal seats.
